query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, pack-cementation aluminide coating to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of an adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 scale that improves its oxygen resistance at high temperatures without degrading its key room‐ and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: A single surface modification via pack-cementation aluminizing to deposit a thin aluminide coating.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours, with the material subsequently subjected to rigorous mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests at room temperature and high-temperature conditions matching the baseline mechanical performance regime).
generation.structural_mediator: A protective, dense, and adherent Al2O3 scale that forms on the coating during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: The aluminizing process deposits aluminum on the surface; upon exposure to oxygen at high temperatures, the aluminum rapidly oxidizes to form a continuous and slow-growing alumina layer. This oxide scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress, thereby mitigating oxidation (and consequently pesting) while preserving the underlying alloy’s microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated material, the aluminized alloy is expected to show significantly reduced oxidation (e.g., lower weight gain and less scale spallation) while maintaining its baseline mechanical strength and ductility under the stated test conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (prone to pesting) despite its favorable mechanical performance at room and high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature oxidation conditions (800 °C for 5 hours exposure in air) and across the mechanical performance boundaries specified (room-temperature tensile ductility of 8–16% and high-temperature yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.uncertainty: While similar non‐equiatomic alloys have benefitted from oxidation protection via surface treatments, the compatibility of the aluminizing process with the equiatomic composition’s phase stability and mechanical properties remains to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group to receive the pack-cementation aluminizing treatment (with optimized processing parameters to yield a uniform aluminide coating) and a control group left untreated. Expose both groups to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Post-exposure, perform weight gain measurements, detailed microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS and XRD to assess the formation and integrity of the Al2O3 scale), and mechanical testing (tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature) to assess mechanical property retention.
measurements: Weight gain per unit area to quantify oxidation rate.
Morphology, thickness, and adherence of the oxide scale via SEM and cross-sectional analysis.
Phase identification of the surface oxide via XRD.
Room-temperature and high-temperature tensile properties (ductility, yield strength).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples show no statistically significant reduction in oxidation (comparable weight gain, scale spallation, or microstructural degradation) and/or if their mechanical properties (room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength) degrade significantly compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis that aluminizing improves oxygen resistance without compromising mechanical performance is falsified.
